title: Burp Session — WSTG-SESS/CRYP: Cookies, JWT, CSRF, Session Management
body: WSTG-SESS has 9 tests (SESS-01 through SESS-09) plus WSTG-SESS-10 for JWT. Session management is where authentication meets persistence — a stolen or forged token is as powerful as the user's password. The five JWT attacks (alg:none, RS256->HS256 confusion, weak secret crack, kid injection, jwk injection) are the highest-severity and most exam-relevant. Cookie attribute audit, CSRF validation in Repeater, and session invalidation after logout round out the category.
cmd:
# ══ ⭐ SESSION TESTING — WSTG-SESS (9 tests) + WSTG-CRYP ══════════════

# 1) COOKIE ATTRIBUTE AUDIT (WSTG-SESS-02) — check EVERY session cookie
# HTTP History -> click any response -> check Set-Cookie headers
curl -si http://$ip/login | grep -i "set-cookie"
# Required attributes:
#   Secure     — MISSING: cookie sent over HTTP = network interception
#   HttpOnly   — MISSING: JS can read it = XSS graduates to session hijack
#   SameSite=Strict or Lax — MISSING: CSRF attacks possible
#   Domain=    — TOO BROAD: .example.com shared across all subdomains
#   Path=/     — MISSING RESTRICTION: accessible to all app paths
# Impact chain:
#   Missing HttpOnly + XSS = steal session cookie -> full account takeover
#   Missing Secure + HTTP available = intercept on the wire
#   Missing SameSite = CSRF (cross-site state-changing request)

# 2) JWT — decode, analyse, and attack (WSTG-SESS-10)
# JWT structure: header.payload.signature (base64url each section)
# Quick decode: echo "eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9" | base64 -d  -> {"alg":"HS256"}
# Or: JWT Editor extension -> paste JWT -> decoded view in JSON Web Token tab
#
# READ THE HEADER first:
#   alg: HS256/HS384/HS512   = HMAC symmetric (shared secret)
#   alg: RS256/RS384/RS512   = RSA asymmetric (private sign, public verify)
#   alg: none                = NO signature -> trivial bypass if accepted
#   kid:                     = key ID -> injection point (path traversal, SQLi)
#
# READ THE PAYLOAD for interesting claims:
#   sub/user_id  (who you are)     role/admin (what you can do)
#   exp          (when it expires) iat (when it was issued)
#
# ATTACK 1 — alg:none (WSTG-SESS-10):
# Remove the signature, set alg to "none" -> server accepts unsigned token
# JWT Editor -> JSON Web Token tab -> alg field -> change to "none"
# Delete the signature (everything after the last .) -> send
# Or manually: echo -n '{"alg":"none","typ":"JWT"}' | base64 -> combine with modified payload

# ATTACK 2 — RS256 -> HS256 key confusion (CRITICAL):
# If server uses RS256 public key to VERIFY, but you switch alg to HS256,
# it uses the PUBLIC KEY as the HMAC secret -> you can sign valid tokens
# JWT Editor -> New Symmetric Key -> paste the public key as the secret
# Change alg from RS256 to HS256 -> sign -> send
# The public key is often at /.well-known/jwks.json or /oauth/certs

# ATTACK 3 — Weak HMAC secret (brute force):
hashcat -m 16500 jwt.txt /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt
# Format: paste the FULL JWT string as the hash (header.payload.signature)
# Common weak secrets: secret, password, admin, changeme, 12345

# ATTACK 4 — kid (Key ID) injection:
# kid is used to select which key to verify with -> inject into the value:
#   "kid":"../../dev/null"  -> verify with empty key -> sign with empty string
#   "kid":"1 UNION SELECT 'secret'-- -" -> SQLi in key lookup
# JWT Editor -> Header -> modify kid field -> sign with the injected key

# ATTACK 5 — jwk header injection:
# JWT header can include the verification key itself (jwk field)
# Attacker generates their own RSA key, embeds it in the header -> signs with it
# JWT Editor -> Attacks -> Embedded JWK (one-click)

# 3) SESSION FIXATION (WSTG-SESS-03)
# Record your session ID BEFORE login. Log in. Record session ID AFTER.
# If the session ID did NOT change -> fixation vulnerability:
#   Attacker sets a known session ID for victim -> victim logs in -> attacker owns session
# Test: get a fresh /login page (no auth) -> note Set-Cookie value
#        log in -> check if the session cookie changed
# In Burp: HTTP History -> find pre-login request + post-login response -> compare

# 4) CSRF — validate the CSRF token properly? (WSTG-SESS-05)
# CSRF token present != CSRF protection. Test if it's actually VALIDATED:
# In Repeater: send a state-changing POST (password change, email update, delete)
#   Test 1: remove the CSRF token entirely -> does it still work? -> NOT validated
#   Test 2: change token to "aaaa" (garbage) -> does it still work? -> NOT validated
#   Test 3: use another user's valid token -> does it work? -> token NOT user-bound
# Rails: the authenticity_token. Laravel: _token. Both SHOULD fail if removed.
# Missing CSRF + SameSite=None + no Secure = full CSRF vulnerability
# Exploit: craft a form on attacker.com that POSTs to victim site -> victim clicks link

# 5) LOGOUT & SESSION INVALIDATION (WSTG-SESS-06)
# After clicking logout, copy the session cookie from before logout
# Make an authenticated request with the OLD cookie -> does it work?
# If YES -> server not invalidating server-side -> session token still valid
# Check: token-based auth (JWT) cannot be server-invalidated unless there's a blacklist
# JWT: check exp claim -> can you use an expired token?
#   In Repeater: set the clock back (change exp to a past timestamp) -> does it reject?

# 6) SESSION TIMEOUT (WSTG-SESS-07)
# Leave an authenticated session idle for 15/30/60 minutes
# Come back -> is the session still valid?
# No timeout = stolen cookie works indefinitely
# Check: what happens when you replay a session token hours after it was issued?

# 7) COOKIE SECURITY TESTING CHECKLIST
# Paste any cookie value into Decoder -> Smart Decode:
#   If it decodes cleanly -> it's not encrypted -> tamper with it
#   Base64 -> JSON? -> try modifying "role":"user" -> "role":"admin"
# Are cookies scoped correctly?
#   Domain=.example.com -> shared with evil.example.com (subdomain takeover risk)
# Predictability: send same login request 10 times -> different cookie each time?
#   If similar/predictable -> Sequencer -> statistical entropy test

# 8) OWASP TOP 10 2021 — A02: Cryptographic Failures (WSTG-CRYP)
# TLS version: does the app accept TLS 1.0/1.1? (deprecated)
nmap --script ssl-enum-ciphers -p 443 $ip
testssl.sh https://$ip     # comprehensive TLS audit
# Sensitive data in URLs: passwords, tokens, session IDs in the query string?
#   GET /reset?token=abc123 -> token in logs, referrer headers, browser history
# Mixed content: HTTPS page loads HTTP resources -> sslstrip opportunity
# In HTTP History: look for responses containing sensitive data patterns:
grep -i "password\|secret\|api_key\|token" in HTTP History responses
warn: alg:none and RS256->HS256 are critical JWT attacks that JWT Editor makes trivial — always test the algorithm. CSRF token PRESENT does not mean CSRF PROTECTED — test whether the token is actually validated by removing it entirely in Repeater. Missing HttpOnly on a session cookie means XSS immediately escalates to full session hijack. Session fixation requires checking whether the session ID CHANGES after login — if it doesn't, the pre-login token is the attack surface.

choices.label: JWT weak secret — crack with hashcat
XSS + missing HttpOnly = hijack the session
